newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Asia-Pacific nations pledge to speed up free trade.
newsitem.headline: Asia-Pacific nations pledge to speed up free trade.

text.p: Asia-Pacific nations meeting in Manila have agreed on what they say is the world's most ambitious plan for lowering trade barriers but concede they lack the ability to guarantee this actually happens.

Detailed country-by-country plans to create the world's biggest free trade region are spelt out in the Manila Action Plan for APEC (MAPA) approved on Friday by trade and foreign ministers of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum.
These plans are so comprehensive they are "without parallel in other trade and investment liberalisation fora", according to an advance copy of the plan obtained by Reuters.

But only five of the 18 member economies have spelt out how they are going to reach APEC's stated goal of lowering all tariff barriers by 2010 for developed members like the United States and Japan and by 2020 for the less well off.
The five are Brunei, Chile, Hong Kong, New Zealand and Singapore.
MAPA also admits that the loose regional grouping, which insists that all agreements should remain voluntary and non-binding, lacks the teeth to enforce these commitments.
"... The challenge is whether the mechanism of consultation, review and revision will in fact deliver," the MAPA says.

U.S. President Bill Clinton, China's Jiang Zemin and Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto and other APEC leaders are expected to endorse MAPA at their summit on Monday at Subic Bay, north of Manila.

Despite the overall failure to match the tariff-free ambitions espoused at the second APEC summit in Bogor, Indonesia, several members have pledged to go beyond their commitments under the World Trade Organisation, the document says.
China, currently seeking membership of the world trade body meeting in Singapore next month, pledges under MAPA to cut its average tariff rate to 15 percent from the current 23 percent by 2000.
MAPA also spells out members' commitments to opening up their service sectors, especially financial services.
China pledges to allow more foreign banks, insurance firms and securities houses to open by 2000.

The action plan details plans to allow faster and cheaper movement of goods in the region by harmonizing customs procedures and working towards a "paperless" computerised system for processing exports and imports.
It cites a United Nations study that found 7-10 percent of the value of goods traded internationally consists of import documentation and other formalities.

MAPA also enshrines the role of the private sector as a "reality check" on APEC and does not overlook the need to spread the region's wealth more equitably by fostering economic and technical cooperation.
